passage:
Mentor meeting note, Tuesday. Divyansh, third year.
Divyansh was quiet today. When I asked about his week, he said he'd been scrolling back through his chat with Mohit, his school friend from Indore, and realised their last proper conversation was in February. It is September now. "We didn't fight or anything," he said. "Nothing happened. That's what's weird. I can't even be angry at anyone."
He said he feels silly being sad about "basically nothing" when other people have real problems. He kept clicking his pen cap on and off.
I told him that a friendship slowly going quiet is still a loss, and it is all right to feel sad about it without a big reason. He looked surprised at that, then a little relieved.
I suggested he could write to Mohit if he wanted, or simply let himself miss him for now. Will check in next week.

qa.q: When was Divyansh's last proper conversation with Mohit?
qa.a: Their last proper conversation was in February.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh feel silly for being sad?
qa.a: Divyansh thinks the sadness has no real cause, since nothing happened and there was no fight, so it feels like being sad about 'basically nothing'.

qa.q: How did the mentor help Divyansh at this stage?
qa.a: The mentor named the fading as a real loss, gave Divyansh permission to feel sad, and offered choices: write to Mohit or simply miss him for now.

qa.q: How might Mohit be experiencing these same months?
qa.a: Mohit may not have noticed the gap at all, or may feel the same quiet sadness without saying it, since there was never any fight.

grounding: Shows a young man realising months have passed since a real talk with his school friend and feeling sad with nothing to blame, and a mentor allowing that grief.

passage:
Sunday night
Santosh posted a photo today from a trek. With people I don't know. And it hit me: I didn't know he'd gone. I didn't even know he liked trekking now.
I scrolled up our chat. Last real message: 12 May, about my cousin's wedding. After that, just birthday wishes and one forwarded joke. Four months.
We didn't fight. Nobody left. There's nothing I can point to and say, that's when. That makes it worse somehow, because who do I tell? "My friend is fine and we just stopped talking"? Sounds like nothing.
But it doesn't feel like nothing. It feels like when Nani's house was sold. Same rooms, just not ours any more.
Maybe I'm allowed to be sad about this. I think I am.
Lalit

qa.q: What was the last real message in the chat about?
qa.a: The last real message was about Lalit's cousin's wedding, on 12 May.

qa.q: Why does the lack of a fight make Lalit feel worse?
qa.a: With nothing to point to, Lalit feels no one would accept it as a reason to be sad, so the hurt has nowhere to go.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next with this sadness?
qa.a: Lalit could let the grief be real, talk about it with someone close, and decide whether to message Santosh about the trek to see what is still worth keeping.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the last four months?
qa.a: Santosh has probably just been busy with new people and trekking and may not see the silence as an ending at all.

grounding: Illustrates quiet grief when a friendship fades with no single event to blame, a loss that feels hard to mourn openly.
